headline: Cloudy Monday with patchy fog, then wetter, windier weather Wednesday through Friday, with possibly heavy rain next weekend.
summary: As of Sunday evening, high pressure keeps western Washington dry but cloudy through Monday morning. Clouds are already filling back in, and leftover moisture could produce patchy fog, especially in fog-prone areas, which may limit visibility on the Monday morning commute. Forecasters call it a tough call between fog and a low cloud deck, and light easterly winds may cut down fog in some spots. Clearing probably won't come until the afternoon. Overnight lows were raised to above freezing in the Southwest Interior because clouds are already there. Light showers offshore should move inland Monday evening, but amounts will be very light. By Tuesday afternoon it turns drier and slightly warmer, though sunny breaks may be few, with temperatures near normal or a few degrees above. Wednesday brings widespread rain and high-elevation snow, mostly over the Olympic Peninsula and North Cascades, with very little rain east of the Olympics. A stronger system follows into Friday morning, with about a half inch to an inch of water in the mountains, a tenth or two of an inch in the lowlands, and a few inches of new snow at higher elevations. Next weekend could bring the heaviest rain of the fall so far, but details are uncertain, and the second week of November is highly uncertain. No watches, warnings, or advisories are in effect for land areas. A Small Craft Advisory for the coastal waters and the west end of the Strait of Juan de Fuca runs from 1 AM Monday to 1 AM Tuesday because of building seas of 8 to 11 feet.
changes: The overnight Dense Fog Advisory ended, and forecasters moved from expecting widespread, possibly dense fog Monday morning to patchy fog or low cloud. Later discussions also added specifics for the Wednesday to Friday systems and raised the possibility of heavy rain next weekend.
